title: Dhaka asks UK for help on Myanmar as London puts £400m into climate fund
excerpt: The British High Commissioner announced a £400 million UK contribution to a new Climate Investment Funds mechanism. The two sides also discussed early warning and climate displacement.

image.alt: Monsoon clouds over flooded fields in Bangladesh
image.credit: File photo: lensnmatter / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0

content:
British High Commissioner Sarah Cooke announced the UK's first contribution of £400 million to a new Climate Investment Funds (CIF) mechanism that aims to attract private money into clean energy, The Business Standard reported, citing the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. She was meeting State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam in Dhaka on Monday (23 November).

The talks followed up on meetings at the COP31 climate conference. The two sides discussed drawing more climate investment to Bangladesh, and cooperation on early warning systems, climate displacement, the effect of climate change on women and children, and natural fibres such as jute.

Shama Obaed welcomed the International Court of Justice judgment that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya and asked London to help increase international pressure on Myanmar to carry it out. Cooke said the UK would keep supporting Rohingya return to Myanmar that is "safe, voluntary, dignified and sustainable."

Why it matters

The ministry's statement does not say how much of the £400 million could reach Bangladesh. CIF money mostly flows through multilateral banks, so climate NGOs and local adaptation groups are unlikely to see it directly. Early warning and climate displacement, both on the agenda, are areas where Bangladeshi NGOs already work with UK funding.

What to watch

Whether Bangladesh is named as a country for the new CIF mechanism, and any new UK funding for the Rohingya response after the ICJ ruling.
